lessons.title: Making Connections
lessons.problem: RI.K.3 is connecting two individuals/events/ideas in a text; this lesson quietly drifts into cause-and-effect only. The teach example (sun is hot, plants need sun) and the caterpillar example mix loose 'relatedness' with causation, so the through-line of what 'connection' means is a little muddy for a 5-year-old.

steps.ttsScript: In fact books, different pieces of information are connected to each other, like puzzle pieces!
When we make connections, we figure out how two things go together. Like how rain helps flowers grow!
Let's learn how to connect facts!
Sometimes one fact helps explain another fact.
Like: The sun is hot. Plants need the sun to grow. See? The sun connects to the plants!
Connections help us understand why things happen and how things are related!
Listen to these facts and find the connection!
Caterpillars eat lots of leaves.
Then caterpillars turn into butterflies!
The connection? Eating leaves helps the caterpillar grow so it can become a butterfly!
There are a few special words that tell us how ideas connect. Each one tells you something different!
because. Tells you WHY!
so. Tells you WHAT HAPPENED!
then. Tells you WHAT COMES NEXT!
You're a connection master!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to these facts. It was a sunny day. The snow melted quickly. Why did the snow melt?

interactive.hint: Think about how the facts connect. What caused the snow to melt?

steps.ttsScript: Amazing work! You know how to connect facts like a pro!
Let's practice making connections. Let's go!

lessons.title: Parts of a Book
lessons.problem: Only 1 practice MCQ (vs. 5 in the siblings), so the kid gets almost no independent reps after instruction; the lesson also slightly overstuffs the teach slide with four parts at once before any practice.

currentSlides.heading: Let's Learn About Parts of a Book!

steps.ttsScript: Did you know a book has special parts, just like your body has parts?
There's a front cover, a back cover, and the title page! Each part tells you something important.
Let's learn what each part does!
The front cover is the very first thing you see. It has the title and usually a picture!
The title tells you what the book is about. It's like the book's name!
The back cover is on the other side. It might tell you a little bit about the book.
The title page is inside the book. It shows the title, author, and illustrator!
Let's try one together! Here's a new book.
This book is called All About Bugs.
What part shows the title and a picture? The front cover!
Where do we find who made it? The title page inside!
The front cover greets you, and the title page tells who made it. You're a book expert!
Look at this book. Can you find the front cover?
There it is! The front cover has a whale and says 'Ocean Animals.' That's the title!
If we flip it over, we see the back cover!
And if we open it up, we see the title page inside!
Every time you pick up a new book, check out the parts first!
Look at the front cover to learn what the book is about. Check the title page for who made it!
You'll be a book expert in no time!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Lily picked up a book. She saw a big picture of a dog and the words 'My Best Friend' on the very first part. What part of the book did Lily see?

interactive.hint: Think about the very first part of a book you see.

steps.ttsScript: Great work learning the parts of a book!
Let's practice identifying book parts. You know this stuff!

lessons.title: Reasons and Support
lessons.problem: the 'Your Turn' Leo item is really find-a-detail, not identify-a-reason-that-supports-a-point, so it drifts from the actual standard

steps.ttsScript: Sometimes an author tells us something and then explains WHY. Those are called reasons!
Reasons help us understand why the author thinks something is true.
Let's learn how to find reasons in what we read!
An author might say: Dogs make great pets. But why? They need to give us reasons!
Reasons are the facts that back up what the author says.
Like: Dogs are loyal. Dogs are fun to play with. Those are reasons why dogs are great pets!
Listen to this and find the reasons!
Fruit is good for you. It gives you energy. It has vitamins. It tastes yummy!
steps.displayText: Fruit is good for you. It gives you energy. It has vitamins. It tastes yummy!

steps.ttsScript: The big idea is 'fruit is good for you.' And the reasons are energy, vitamins, and yummy taste!
When an author says something, look for the word 'because' or look for examples.
Those are usually the reasons! They explain why the author's point makes sense.
You're a reason finder now!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this little story. My friend Leo loves to play outside. He likes to run fast. He also likes to climb trees. And he can jump really high! What is one reason Leo loves to play outside?

interactive.hint: Think about what Leo does when he plays outside.

steps.ttsScript: Fantastic job learning about reasons!
Let's practice finding the reasons authors give. You'll be awesome at this!

lessons.title: Vowel Sounds
lessons.problem: Tries to teach too much for one K lesson — short vs long vowels AND Magic E AND 'every word needs a vowel' — yet the interactive only checks identifying a vowel in 'fish', so the harder concepts go unpracticed and may overwhelm

steps.ttsScript: There are five super special letters called vowels!
First, the letter A.
Next, E.
Then, I.
Now, O.
And finally, U.
These are your five vowels! Let's learn more about them.
Each vowel makes a short sound. A is for apple.
E is for egg. I is for igloo.
O is for octopus. U is for umbrella.
Five vowels, five sounds! A, E, I, O, U!
Vowels can make two sounds: a short sound and a long sound.
The short A sound. Like in cat.
The long A sound. Like in cake. The long sound says its name!
Hear the difference? Cat. Cake. Short A and long A.
Here is a magic trick called Magic E.
Look. We have the word cap. Cap has a short A sound.
Watch this magic! Add an E to the end. Cap becomes cape. The E is silent, but it makes the A say its name.
That is Magic E. Silent at the end, but it changes the vowel sound!
Which vowel do you hear in the word 'cat'?
The vowel in cat is A.
What about 'dog'? The vowel is O.
Here is a helpful trick about vowels.
Every single word must have at least one vowel! A, E, I, O, U.
That is why these five letters are super important. Every word needs one!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this word: fish. Which vowel do you hear in the word 'fish'?

interactive.hint: Listen carefully for the vowel sound in 'fish'. Which letter makes that sound?

steps.ttsScript: You know your vowels! That's a big deal!
Let's practice hearing vowel sounds in words. Ready? Let's go!

lessons.title: Using New Words
lessons.problem: the Your Turn tests synonym/comprehension (which word means big) rather than the taught skill of USING a new word in a sentence

steps.ttsScript: You learn new words all the time! But the best part is using them!
When you use new words when you talk and write, your vocabulary grows bigger and bigger!
Let's practice using new words in sentences!
When you learn a new word, try to use it right away! Say it in a sentence!
Like if you learn the word 'enormous,' try saying: That building is enormous!
The more you use a word, the better you remember it!
Pretty soon, new words become YOUR words!
Here's a new word: 'delighted.' It means really, really happy!
Can you use it in a sentence? How about: I was delighted to see my friend!
See? You just used a brand new word! You're a vocabulary superstar!
Every time you learn a new word, use it three times that day!
Use it talking to a friend, use it in a sentence you write, and use it at home!
Three times and that word is yours forever!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this little story. Lily went to the farm and saw a pumpkin. It was so big, she could barely roll it! What word from our lesson describes that pumpkin?

interactive.hint: Think about the new words we learned. Which one means very, very big?

steps.ttsScript: You're growing your vocabulary every day!
Let's practice using new words in the right way. Let's go!

lessons.title: Retelling Stories
lessons.problem: the Your Turn only asks to identify the problem (the middle), not to retell/sequence B-M-E, which is the real skill

steps.ttsScript: Retelling means telling a story in your own words.
You keep the most important parts.
And you leave out the tiny details.
Every story has three big parts.
The beginning. Who is in the story and what is happening?
The middle. What is the problem or the big event?
The end. How does it all work out?
Listen. Tom wanted to win the race. He practiced every day. On race day, he came in first!
steps.displayText: Tom wanted to win the race. He practiced every day. On race day, he came in first!

steps.ttsScript: Beginning. Tom wanted to win a race.
steps.displayText: Tom wanted to win a race.

steps.ttsScript: Middle. He practiced every single day.
End. He won! The lesson? Practice helps!
Many stories teach a lesson.
Ask yourself, what did the character learn? That is the lesson.
Now you are ready to practice retelling stories!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this story. Lily loved to draw pictures. One day, her favorite red crayon broke in half! So, she decided to use her colorful paints instead. What was the problem in the story?

interactive.hint: Think about what happened in the middle of the story.

lessons.title: Words That Show Feelings
lessons.problem: the Your Turn answer 'Tears' is a noun/thing, not the kind of vivid feeling-word the lesson just modeled, so the item undercuts the teaching

steps.ttsScript: Writers choose special words to make us feel something.
Some words help us hear, see, or touch a story in our mind.
Let us find some feeling words!
Today, we will learn about words that tell us how characters feel.
Words like happy, excited, or joyful show us good feelings.
Other words like sad, angry, or scared tell us when characters have different feelings.
These feeling words help us understand what is happening in a story.
Watch how one word changes everything. Here is a plain sentence: She walked to the door.
Now I will swap in a feeling word. She stomped to the door. Stomped makes me feel that she is angry! The very same girl, but one word tells me how she feels inside.
Listen. The bright sun warmed her face.
steps.displayText: The bright sun warmed her face.

steps.ttsScript: Which word helps us feel the sun? Warmed!
That word makes us feel the sun on our own skin.
Here is a helpful trick.
When you read a feeling word, stop and feel it for a moment.
Now you are ready to practice finding feeling words!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Read this sentence. Big tears rolled down her cheeks. Which word shows us she feels sad?

interactive.hint: Which word makes you feel it?

lessons.title: Parts of a Fact Book
lessons.problem: teaches three text features but only tests one (TOC); no worked example, so it names parts more than it models using them to find info

steps.ttsScript: Fact books are built with special parts to help you find stuff.
Once you know the parts, finding facts is fast!
Let us meet them!
The table of contents is up front.
It lists every chapter and what page it starts on.
Want chapter three? Look here first!
A heading is the big words at the top of a page.
It tells you what that page is about.
Labels are little words that point to parts of a picture.
Here is a helpful trick.
Before you read, look at the headings and pictures. They tell you what is coming!
Now you are ready to find facts using book parts!

currentSlides.heading: Fact Book Parts
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Imagine you want to find a specific chapter in a fact book. Where would you look to see a list of all the chapters and their page numbers?

interactive.hint: Think about where you look first to find a chapter.

lessons.title: Word Beginnings and Endings
lessons.problem: The tip slide abruptly switches to a third affix (-ed) that was never taught in the teach slides and isn't practiced, so it crams in an unmodeled concept; the lesson teaches un-/-er but the tip muddies the focus

steps.ttsScript: Little word parts can change what a word means.
They stick on the beginning or the end.
Let us meet a few!
The ending E R can mean one who does.
Teacher? One who teaches!
Runner? One who runs!
The beginning U N means not.
Unhappy? Not happy!
Unlock? Not locked!
Here is a helpful trick to understand long words.
Sometimes, little parts at the end of a word can change its meaning.
The word 'jump' means to leap. When we add the ending '-ed', it becomes 'jumped', meaning it already happened!
Now you know how word endings can give you clues about what a word means!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! If UN means not, what does the word 'unfold' mean?

interactive.hint: Remember, the word part UN means not.

lessons.title: Using Big Words
lessons.problem: The example beat is filler ('use new words') rather than a modeled application, leaving the teaching a bit abstract

steps.ttsScript: Great readers and writers pick the just-right word.
The right word makes a sentence clear!
Let us practice.
When you read a sentence with a blank, think about what fits.
The kids were hungry. They ate a ___.
steps.displayText: The kids were hungry. They ate a ___.

steps.ttsScript: A banquet? Yes! A symphony? No!
Every day, you learn new words from books and talks.
Try using them! The more you use a word, the better you know it.
Big words make your ideas shine!
Here is a helpful trick.
Ask, does this word fit the meaning of my sentence?
Now you are ready to use big words!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this sentence: The little puppy was so tiny. It was very... which word best fits the blank?

interactive.hint: Think about what 'tiny' means.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Story
lessons.problem: The teaching is thin and abstract — it tells kids what each part does but never models it on an actual story before the interactive, so there's no worked example bridging the explanation to the 'Your Turn'; a child weak on this would jump from definitions straight to application

steps.ttsScript: Every story has a shape. A beginning, middle, and end.
The shape helps us follow along.
Let us look at each part.
The beginning introduces us. Who is the story about? Where are they?
It sets up the whole story.
The middle is where most of the action happens.
There is usually a problem or a big event.
The end wraps things up. How did it all turn out?
Here is a helpful trick.
As you read, ask: am I in the beginning, middle, or end?
Now you are ready to see the shape of a story!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, story detective! Listen to this little story: Lily the squirrel woke up hungry. She saw a big acorn under an oak tree. She ran to get it. Suddenly, a big black crow swooped down! The crow wanted the acorn too. Lily chattered loudly and held on tight. Finally, the crow flew away, and Lily buried her acorn safely. In this story, what part is it when the crow swooped down?

interactive.hint: Remember, the middle is where the problem or big event happens.

lessons.title: Finding the Big Idea
lessons.problem: The Your Turn distractors are weak: 'Dogs' vs 'Playing fetch'/'Training tricks' lets a kid pick the answer just by spotting the most-repeated noun rather than by synthesizing the big idea, so it under-tests the skill it just taught

steps.ttsScript: Longer fact texts have lots of little ideas.
But one big idea holds them all together.
That big idea is called the main topic.
Each paragraph focuses on a smaller part of the big idea.
Paragraph one might tell what something is.
Paragraph two might tell why it matters.
All paragraphs point back to the main topic.
Imagine a text about honey bees.
One paragraph on how they make honey. Another on where they live.
steps.displayText: One paragraph on how they make honey. Another on where they live.

steps.ttsScript: Main topic? Honey bees! Everything connects back to them.

currentSlides.heading: Ask What It Is All About

steps.ttsScript: Here is a helpful trick.
After you read, ask: what is this text mostly about?
Now you are ready to find the big idea!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to this short text. 'Dogs love to play fetch and run in the park. They can learn to sit, stay, and roll over. Many families keep dogs as pets because they are loyal and fun.' What's the big idea of this text?

interactive.hint: Think about what all the sentences are mostly about.

lessons.title: How Authors Back Up Their Points
lessons.problem: the Your Turn asks for the main point, not the reasons that support it, so the guided practice tests main-idea rather than RI.2.8's actual skill

steps.ttsScript: When an author makes a point, they also give reasons.
The reasons back up the point.
Spotting them makes you a strong reader!
Point: you should drink water every day.
Reason one: it helps your body work.
Reason two: it keeps you from getting tired.
Two reasons support the point!
Point: riding bikes is fun and healthy.
Reasons? Exercise. Fresh air. Going places fast!
The reasons make the point stronger.
Here is a helpful trick.
Watch for words like because, since, and for example. Those signal reasons!
Now you are ready to spot author's reasons!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely to this story. 'You should always eat breakfast. It gives you energy for the whole day. Plus, it helps you think clearly and learn a lot in school!' What is the author's main point?

interactive.hint: Think about what the author wants you to do or believe.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Fact Books
lessons.problem: the Your Turn compares two kids talking about pets rather than two texts on a topic, and only asks for the similarity, never the contrast, so it doesn't model comparing two books

steps.ttsScript: Two fact books can be about the same topic.
But each author picks different details.
Reading both gives you a bigger picture.
Look for what both books agree on.
Those are the main points everyone knows.
Then look for what is special in each one.
One might share more pictures. The other more stories.
Both add to what you know!
Here is a helpful trick.
Make a two-column chart. Same on one, different on the other.
Now you are ready to compare two fact books!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Mia and Leo were talking about their pets. Mia said her cat, Whiskers, loves to chase string. Leo said his cat, Mittens, loves to nap in sunny spots. But they both agreed that cats are soft. What is something both Mia and Leo said about their cats?

interactive.hint: Think about what was the same in both stories.

lessons.title: Reading Facts All Year
lessons.problem: by nature it can't truly 'teach' year-long reading proficiency, so it leans motivational over skill-building

steps.ttsScript: Reading fact books all year makes you smarter.
Different topics build different knowledge.
Pick fact books about things you love.
Animals, sports, space, food, weather. Anything!
Love makes it fun.
Sometimes, try reading informational books that are a little harder.
These stretch books help you understand more facts and ideas.
Let's try one together. Here's a short fact.
The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.
steps.displayText: The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.

steps.ttsScript: What is the sun? A huge star!
What does it give us? Light and heat!
You found two facts about the sun. Fact books make you smarter!
Here is a helpful trick.
Try a new topic each week. You will discover something cool!
Now you are ready to read facts all year!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Here's a thinking one! Ben already read three whole books about sharks. He knows every shark fact now. What should Ben try next to learn even more?

interactive.hint: Remember the trick about a new topic.

lessons.title: Tricky Spellings
lessons.problem: it's a grab-bag (silent letters + PH lumped together) and the tip is a study habit, not a transferable decoding skill

steps.ttsScript: Some spellings are tricky. Letters hide or change sound!
These are surprises English throws at us.
Let us learn a few common ones.
In knee, the K is silent.
In lamb, the B is silent.
In write, the W is silent too!
When P and H team up, they make the F sound!
Phone. Photo. Dolphin. All PH words that sound like F.
Let's try one together. Here's a tricky word.
Here is the word: thumb.
Which letter is silent and hides? The B!
Do we say it out loud? No, it stays silent!
So thumb sounds like thum. The B is just for show. You caught the surprise!
Here is a helpful trick.
When a word surprises you, write it down. Then practice it a few times!
Now you are ready to read tricky spellings!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Look at these words. Can you match each word to its tricky spelling rule?

interactive.hint: Think about which letter is silent or which letters make a new sound.

lessons.title: Using Smart Words
lessons.problem: the proud/joyful/thrilled discrimination is too subtle for grade 2 and the 'correct' answer is debatable

steps.ttsScript: When you learn a new word, use it!
The more you use a word, the more it sticks.

currentSlides.heading: Match Your Words to the Moment

steps.ttsScript: Different situations call for different words.
Talking to a friend? Use chill words.
Writing an essay? Use fancier ones.
Instead of happy, you could say joyful, thrilled, or proud.
Each one paints a slightly different picture!

currentSlides.heading: Try a New Word Each Day

steps.ttsScript: Here is a helpful trick.
Pick one new word each day. Use it in a sentence!
Now you are ready to use smart words!

currentSlides.heading: Smart Word Choice
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, word detective! Maya finished a really hard puzzle all by herself and held it up high. Which word best paints how she felt?

interactive.hint: She did something hard all by herself.

lessons.title: Parts of Stories and Poems
lessons.problem: It is pure term-labeling — the kid never sees a real stanza, scene, or chapter in context and never touches 'how each part builds on the one before,' which is the heart of RL.3.5

steps.ttsScript: Stories, plays, and poems are organized into parts.
Knowing the parts helps us talk about them.
Chapters divide a story into bigger parts.
Plays use scenes instead of chapters.
Poems use lines and stanzas.
A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in a poem.
Here is a helpful trick.
When talking about stories, use words like chapter, scene, line, or stanza!
Now you are ready to name the parts of stories and poems!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Now you try! Match each part to the kind of writing it belongs to.

interactive.prompt: Match the part to its form
interactive.hint: Poems have stanzas, plays have scenes, stories have chapters.

lessons.title: Connecting Events and Ideas
lessons.problem: Standard is about connecting events/ideas (cause-effect, sequence, comparison) but the example only teaches cause-effect, then the Your Turn tests sequence ordering — a mismatch that leaves the modeled skill (cause-effect) untested and the tested skill (sequence) only briefly taught

steps.ttsScript: Events and ideas in nonfiction often connect.
Cause and effect. Sequence. Compare and contrast.
One thing causes another. The water spilled because the glass tipped.
Look for because, so, as a result.
Sequence is the order of events.
First, next, then, finally.
Let's try one together. Here's a true event.
The plant wilted because nobody watered it for a week.
steps.displayText: The plant wilted because nobody watered it.

steps.ttsScript: What signal word connects them? Because!
What caused it? No water made the plant wilt.
No water caused the plant to wilt. You connected cause and effect!
Here is a helpful trick.
Draw boxes and arrows to show how events connect.
Now you are ready to connect events and ideas!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Here's the order: The bird felt hungry. Then it flew to the feeder. Then it ate the seeds. Then its tummy was full. Which event happened FIRST?

interactive.hint: First comes before next.

lessons.title: Author's Point of View
lessons.problem: The 'example' is an abstract three-step procedure (author's view / your view / compare) with no actual text to apply it to — it tells the strategy instead of modeling it on a real passage, weakening the bridge to the otherwise solid Your Turn

steps.ttsScript: Every author has a point of view.
You have your own view too. Notice when you agree or disagree.
Words like best, most important, or should signal opinion.
Those are the author's view, not your view!

currentSlides.heading: Your View vs. The Author's View

steps.ttsScript: When we read, we first think about what the author believes or feels about the topic.
Then, we think about what we believe or feel about the same topic.
Finally, we compare to see if our ideas are similar to the author's or if they are different.
Here is a helpful trick.
Circle opinion words as you read. That is where the author shows their view.
Now you are ready to spot author's view!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely. 'Everyone should visit the lake. You should pack a lunch and stay all day. You will never want to leave!' How does the author feel about the lake?

interactive.hint: Opinion words like 'should' show the author's feeling.

lessons.title: Reading Facts All Year
lessons.problem: RI.3.10 is a range/stamina standard ('read and comprehend informational texts at the high end of the grade band') — it isn't a discrete skill, and the lesson papers over that by re-teaching main-idea/detail (RI.3.2) instead; also the correct answer 'Bats are amazing' is a vague title-feel answer that competes awkwardly with the more concrete distractors.

steps.ttsScript: Fact books all year keep your brain growing.
This year, we will read and understand longer fact books.
These books will teach you many new things and help you comprehend more.
Try new topics
Science.History.
Sports.Cooking.
Let's try one together. Here's a short fact passage.
Bees live in hives. They make sweet honey.
What is it mostly about? The main idea is bees!
What is one important detail about it? They make honey!
Main idea bees, detail honey. You understood the facts!
To understand facts in books, we have a special toolkit of reading tips!
First, look for the main idea, which is what the text is mostly about.
Next, find important details that tell you more about the main idea.
Also, use text features like headings and pictures to help you understand.
With these tips, you are ready to read and understand facts all year long!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn to be the thinker! Listen to this little fact book. Bats are amazing animals. They sleep upside down. They catch bugs in the dark. They can even fly! What is the book mostly about?

interactive.hint: One idea covers the whole book.

lessons.title: Latin Suffixes
lessons.problem: the 'from Latin' framing is decorative and never pays off; intro hook is hollow and the suffix set is a bit arbitrary

steps.ttsScript: Some suffixes come from Latin, a very old language.
Learning them unlocks lots of big words.
TION makes a verb into a noun. Act becomes action.
Celebrate becomes celebration. Create becomes creation.
ABLE or IBLE means able to.
Readable. Washable. Possible. Visible.
Here is a helpful trick.
When you see TION, ABLE, or IBLE, you already know part of the meaning!
Now you are ready for Latin suffixes!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this word: washable. What does 'washable' mean?

interactive.hint: Remember what the suffix -able means.

lessons.title: Using a Dictionary
lessons.problem: No modeled example slide ('Let's Try One') — it tells about dictionaries but never models an actual lookup, and the 'Your Turn' (how are words organized?) is a trivial recall question, so the kid never practices the real skill of finding/reading an entry

steps.ttsScript: Dictionaries tell you meaning.
They also teach you pronunciation.
And how to use a word.
Dictionaries are alphabetical.
Find the first letter,
then the next letter.
Each entry has the word.
Next, it tells you how to say it.
And finally, the meaning.
Here is a helpful trick.
The two words at the top of the page show the first and last word on it. Use them to skim fast!
Now you are ready to use a dictionary!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Dictionaries have a special way of organizing words so you can find them easily. How are words organized in a dictionary?

interactive.hint: Remember how dictionaries help you find words quickly.

lessons.title: Finding Story Details
lessons.problem: the 'example' step only tells about inferring and never works through a passage, so the skill is quizzed without first being modeled

steps.ttsScript: Fourth grade readers use specific details from the text as evidence.
These details are used as evidence to support what the text says.
So, remember: details are evidence!
When you make a claim, quote the exact words from the text.
This helps you show exactly where your information comes from and makes your claims stronger.
Remember to always use quotation marks around the words you take directly from the text.
Sometimes the answer is not stated directly.
We infer it from the details.
To infer means to put clues together.
Here is a helpful trick.
When you answer, say: the text says... and quote a line!
Now you are ready to find story details!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen carefully to this short story. Lily pulled on her thickest sweater and wrapped a long scarf around her neck. She grabbed her mittens before heading out the door. What is the weather like outside?

interactive.hint: Look for clues in the story to figure out the weather.

lessons.title: Poems, Drama, and Prose
lessons.problem: No modeled example slide at all — it jumps from bare definitions straight to the kid's turn, so nothing demonstrates HOW to identify a form before they're asked to; poetry and prose are never shown, only drama.

steps.ttsScript: Stories come in three big forms.
These forms are poems,
drama, and prose.
Poems have lines, stanzas, and often rhythm or rhyme.
Drama is meant to be acted out. It uses scenes and dialogue.
Prose is regular sentences and paragraphs.
Here is a helpful trick.
Use the right words for each form: stanza, scene, paragraph.
Now you are ready to know poems, drama, and prose!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Read this part. Scene One. Max walks in and says, Hello! Then Mia answers. Which story form is this?

interactive.hint: Look for scenes and spoken lines.

lessons.title: Different Storytelling Voices
lessons.problem: Skips the modeled example, so the kid sees definitions and then is immediately tested; it also conflates 'voice' with point of view loosely and never distinguishes third-limited vs third-omniscient, which RL.4.6 actually targets.

steps.ttsScript: Stories can be told in different voices.
First person uses I. Third person uses he, she, they.
First person makes you feel close to the character.
Third person feels more like watching from outside.
The narrator is an observer, not a character in the story.
You'll often see third-person pronouns like 'he', 'she', 'it', or 'they', or character names being used.
Here is a helpful trick.
Look at the pronouns in the first sentence. They tell you the voice.
Now you are ready to spot storytelling voices!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen carefully to this short story. 'I walked to the park today. My dog, Buster, pulled on his leash. We saw a squirrel, and I laughed when Buster barked at it.' Now, what voice is this story told in?

interactive.hint: Listen for who is telling the story.

lessons.title: Stories Across Mediums
lessons.problem: Thin on the actual standard — RL.4.7 is about how a visual/oral presentation reflects specific text descriptions, but the lesson stays at a generic 'movies cut and add scenes' level and never models connecting a specific text moment to its visual realization.

steps.ttsScript: A story can be a book, a movie, a play, or even a song.
Each medium tells the story differently.
A movie shows you visuals and sounds directly.
A book lets you imagine them.
Movies often cut parts of the book to fit the time.
Sometimes they add scenes too!
Here is a helpful trick.
Make a list of what is same and what is different between book and movie.
Now you are ready to compare stories across mediums!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to this tiny story. Tom was reading a book about a bustling city. He imagined the tall buildings, busy streets, and loud taxis. Now, what would a movie show you directly about that city?

interactive.hint: Remember, movies show you visuals and sounds directly, while books let you imagine them.

lessons.title: Reading Big Stories
lessons.problem: It teaches reading-stamina study skills, not comprehension of complex text — it sidesteps what the standard is actually about

steps.ttsScript: Fourth graders take on longer, more complex stories.
Chapter books, novels, and longer poems!
Long books need a steady pace.
A chapter or two a day works great.
Take quick notes
about characters
and big events.
Let's try one together. Here's how a reader takes on a long book.
Sam read one chapter each night. He jotted notes about the brave knight.
steps.displayText: Sam read one chapter each night. He jotted notes about the brave knight.

steps.ttsScript: How much did Sam read each day? One chapter. A steady pace makes a long book easy.
What did he take notes about? The knight, a character he wants to remember.
A chapter a day plus notes on characters. Now you can conquer big stories!
Here is a helpful trick.
Daily reading turns hard books into easy adventures over time!
Now you are ready for big stories!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Lily started reading a very long book. She decided to read just one chapter every day. As she read, she made sure to write down the names of the people in the story so she wouldn't forget them. What did Lily write about?

interactive.hint: Think about what Lily wanted to remember from the story.

lessons.title: Finding Fact Details
lessons.problem: The inference half of the standard is asserted in a 3-word pill with no modeled example, and the Your Turn only tests literal recall

steps.ttsScript: Fourth grade nonfiction readers back up answers with text evidence.
Quote the exact words or summarize the line.
Let's try one together. Listen for the details that prove the answer.
Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.
steps.displayText: Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.

steps.ttsScript: When do bats hunt? At night. The text says so right there.
How do you know? Because the text says they hunt at night. That's your evidence.
You backed your answer with text evidence. That's how detectives read nonfiction!
Sometimes the answer is implied.
Use details to infer it.
Implied = infer
Here is a helpful trick.
Always say: according to the text, before your answer.
Now you are ready to find fact details!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely to this story. Squeaky the squirrel scurried up the oak tree. He carefully tucked his acorns and walnuts into a hollow log. He wanted to save them for winter. What did Squeaky hide?

interactive.hint: Look for the specific details in the story.

lessons.title: How Texts Are Built
lessons.problem: the lesson teaches compare/contrast and problem/solution but the modeled example demonstrates sequence — a structure barely introduced — so the teaching and the model are misaligned

steps.ttsScript: Texts are organized in patterns.
One common pattern is cause and effect.
Other patterns include sequence and problem and solution.
Compare and contrast structure
shows similarities
and differences.
Problem and solution texts
state an issue,
then show how to fix it.
Let's try one together. Listen to this short passage.
First, mix the flour. Next, add eggs. Finally, bake the cake.
steps.displayText: First, mix the flour. Next, add eggs. Finally, bake the cake.

steps.ttsScript: What clue words do you hear? First, next, finally!
What text structure is it? Sequence!
So the clue words tell us it is sequence. You spotted the structure!
Here is a helpful trick.
Words like however, also, because, and finally signal the structure.
Now you are ready to spot text structures!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to this little story. A squirrel couldn't reach the nuts on the high branch. So, it found a long stick and used it to knock the nuts down. What text structure did I just use?

interactive.hint: Think about if there was an issue and how it was fixed.

lessons.title: Information Across Forms
lessons.problem: the teaching stays abstract ('combine all information,' 'full picture') with no actual modeled example integrating two real sources, so the core RI.4.7 skill of synthesizing across forms is never demonstrated

steps.ttsScript: Information can come in text, charts, or diagrams.
It can also be presented through photos or videos.
A chart shows numbers.
A photo shows something real.
Words explain.
To truly understand a topic, we need to combine all the information we gather.
This means looking at details from text, images, charts, and even spoken words.
By putting all these pieces together, we truly get the full picture of the topic.
Here is a helpful trick.
When researching, use multiple sources. They each show different angles.
Now you are ready to use info from many forms!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, researcher! You want to compare how many birds of each kind visited your feeder. Which form would show those amounts best?

interactive.hint: One form is built for comparing numbers.

lessons.title: Author's Reasons and Evidence
lessons.problem: no modeled example at all — it jumps from a thin teach on reasons/evidence straight to the kid's turn, so the link between a point, its reason, and its evidence is never shown in action

steps.ttsScript: Authors give reasons for their points. Strong writers also give evidence.
A reason is the why...
...behind the point.
So, a reason explains why something is true.
Evidence is proof. Facts. Examples. Statistics.
Here is a helpful trick.
Highlight reasons one color and evidence another. See how they connect!
Now you are ready to spot reasons and evidence!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to this story: The park is a great place to play. You can run around and swing on the swings. Yesterday, I saw five kids laughing on the slide and two families having picnics. Now, what is the evidence in this story?

interactive.hint: Remember, evidence is proof or examples that back up a point.

lessons.title: Combining Two Texts
lessons.problem: no worked example before the kid's turn — the integrate-two-texts skill is described abstractly in the teach/tip but never modeled, so the first time it's shown is the question itself

steps.ttsScript: Reading two texts on the same topic
gives a stronger understanding.
Use facts from both texts
to write a stronger summary.
Each text might focus on a different angle.
Notice both.
Let's learn a helpful trick for putting information together from two texts.
First, find key details in each text that answer the same question.
Then, put those details together to form a new, complete understanding.
This helps you speak or write knowledgeably about the topic!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! One article says bees make sweet honey. Another article says bees help flowers grow. When you put both texts together, what do you understand better about bees?

interactive.hint: Put BOTH facts together — what big idea do they show?

lessons.title: Using Big Vocabulary
lessons.problem: The intro/teach is thin and abstract ('use makes them yours', 'casual for chats') with only one concrete word total; a 4th grader gets little actual vocabulary or repeated modeling, so understanding stays shallow

steps.ttsScript: Knowing big words helps. Using them helps even more.
Try new words in your speaking and writing.
They become yours after you use them.
Casual for chats.
Academic for school.
Let's try one together. Here's a big word.
Here is the word: investigate. It means to look into something closely.
Is investigate a casual word or an academic word? Academic!
So where does it fit best? In a school report, not a chat with friends!
You matched a big word to the right setting. That's how smart writers sound clear!
Here is a helpful trick.
One new word a day. Use it three times!
Now you are ready to use big vocabulary!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Imagine you are writing a report about animals for your teacher. What kind of language should you use for your report?

interactive.hint: Think about the setting where you are using the words.

lessons.title: Apostrophes and Commas
lessons.problem: Commas (half the title) appear only in the tip slide with no teach or practice; lesson is lopsided toward apostrophes

steps.ttsScript: Two tiny marks do big jobs in sentences.
Apostrophes and commas.
Let us learn both!
Add an apostrophe and an S to show owning.
The dog's bone. The girl's book.
steps.displayText: The dog's bone. The girl's book.

steps.ttsScript: An apostrophe can also replace missing letters.
Can not becomes can't. Do not becomes don't.
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence.
We want to show the hat belongs to the cat. The cat hat.
What mark shows owning? An apostrophe and an S!
Where does it go? Right after the word cat.
So we write cat's hat. The apostrophe and S show owning. Great work!
Commas separate items in a list.
I like apples, bananas, and grapes!
steps.displayText: I like apples, bananas, and grapes!

steps.ttsScript: Now you are ready to use apostrophes and commas!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: You've got this! When we join two words, an apostrophe stands in for the missing letter. Take the words 'I am'. Which word joins them into one?

interactive.hint: An apostrophe takes the place of a missing letter.

lessons.title: Punctuation Mastery
lessons.problem: intro overpromises (periods, question marks, dialogue, titles) but only compound-sentence commas is actually taught and practiced; the quotation-mark half of the standard is mentioned once and never modeled or assessed

steps.ttsScript: Fourth graders master punctuation rules.
These special marks help us make our writing clear and easy to understand.
Get ready to explore periods, commas, question marks, and more!
When two complete sentences join with and, or, but — use a comma before the conjunction.
I went to the park, and I had fun.
steps.displayText: I went to the park, and I had fun.

steps.ttsScript: Here, the comma comes right before the conjunction 'and', connecting the two complete sentences.
In dialogue, commas and periods go inside the quotation marks.
In titles, capitalize all important words.
For example, in the sentence, 'I love reading,' the comma is inside the quotes.
Let's try one together. Here is a sentence that needs a comma.
Here is the sentence: She ran fast but she fell.
steps.displayText: She ran fast but she fell.

steps.ttsScript: Which word joins the two complete sentences? But! That is the conjunction.
Where does the comma go? Before it! The comma comes right before the conjunction.
So we write: She ran fast, comma, but she fell. Comma before the conjunction. You nailed it!
Here is a helpful trick.
Read your work backwards, sentence by sentence. Catches more errors!
Now you are ready for punctuation mastery!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this sentence: The dog barked and the cat ran away. Where should the comma go to correctly join these two sentences?

interactive.hint: Remember to put the comma before the conjunction.

lessons.title: Storytime All Year
lessons.problem: the Your Turn distractors (close your eyes, skip the pages) are too obviously wrong, so it tests almost no real understanding

steps.ttsScript: Look! Reading stories every day is so much fun.
Each story takes you on a new adventure.
Let us see how to enjoy stories all year long.
There are so many kinds of stories!
Funny ones. Brave ones. Silly ones. Sweet ones.
Try a new kind every week. You will find favorites!
When someone reads to you, listen closely.
Look at the pictures. They are part of the story too!
Ask questions if something is tricky.
After we read a story together, it's fun to talk about it!
You can ask your friend: What was your favorite part of the story and why?
Sharing your ideas helps everyone understand the story even better.
Talking about stories is a great way to learn and have fun with friends!

currentSlides.heading: Your Turn!
currentSlides.spokenQ: Your turn! We learned good ways to enjoy a story. Which one helps you enjoy and understand a story?

interactive.prompt: How do you enjoy a story?
interactive.hint: Think about what helps you understand the story.
